meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In spite of everything, I still believe that people are really good at heart'?
meta.ogDescription: A genuine Anne Frank line from her diary of 15 July 1944 — but usually quoted stripped of its far darker surrounding passage.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Anne Frank wrote this in her diary on Saturday, 15 July 1944, while hiding from the Nazis in the Amsterdam “Secret Annex.” This exact English wording is the 1952 Barbara Mooyaart-Doubleday translation; the later 1995 Susan Massotty “definitive edition” renders the same line “truly good at heart.”

source.excerpt: It’s really a wonder that I haven’t dropped all my ideals, because they seem so absurd and impossible to carry out. Yet I keep them, because in spite of everything I still believe that people are really good at heart.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced material, dating it to the diary entry of 15 July 1944 and noting both the “really” and “truly good at heart” renderings.
The Anne Frank House documents that the first English edition, The Diary of a Young Girl, was translated by B. M. Mooyaart-Doubleday and published in 1952 — the source of the famous English wording.
The original Dutch Het Achterhuis was published in 1947; the 1995 “definitive edition” by Susan Massotty renders the same sentence “truly good at heart.”
source.excerptNote: The 1952 Mooyaart-Doubleday translation of the 15 July 1944 entry. Anne then continues: “I simply can’t build up my hopes on a foundation consisting of confusion, misery, and death.”

author.name: Anne Frank
author.heading: About Anne Frank
author.bio: Annelies Marie “Anne” Frank (1929–1945) was a German-born Jewish girl who kept a diary while hiding with her family in a concealed annex in Amsterdam during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Betrayed in August 1944, she was deported and died at Bergen-Belsen in early 1945, aged 15. Her father Otto, the family’s sole survivor, published her diary as Het Achterhuis in 1947; it has since become one of the most widely read books in the world.

misattribution.heading: The catch: it’s real, but rarely quoted whole
misattribution.intro: The words are authentically Anne Frank’s. What gets distorted is the context and the exact wording — the line is almost always lifted away from the bleak sentences around it and the play/film that made it a slogan.

items.why: The popular English form — “really good at heart” — is the 1952 Mooyaart-Doubleday translation. The 1995 Massotty “definitive edition” renders the same Dutch as “truly good at heart,” so both circulate as if interchangeable.

Frances Goodrich and Albert Hackett’s Pulitzer-winning 1955 stage adaptation and its 1959 film both ended on this line, cementing it as an uplifting “message” — a framing later attacked as sentimentalizing a diary that ends in deportation and death, by Bruno Bettelheim in “The Ignored Lesson of Anne Frank” (Harper’s, November 1960) and Cynthia Ozick in “Who Owns Anne Frank?” (The New Yorker, 6 October 1997).

misattribution.truthLine: Anne Frank genuinely wrote it on 15 July 1944 — immediately adding, “I simply can’t build up my hopes on a foundation consisting of confusion, misery, and death,” a line the slogan version usually drops.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Anne Frank wrote this passage on 15 July 1944 — just weeks before the annex was raided on 4 August 1944 and its occupants deported. Read in full, the entry is not a simple affirmation of human goodness but a young woman arguing with her own despair: she calls her ideals “absurd and impossible to carry out,” yet refuses to abandon them.

Because her father Otto was the only member of the household to survive, the diary reached the world as her voice alone. The single sentence about people being “good at heart” became its emblem — which is precisely why scholars caution that quoting it without the surrounding darkness turns a wartime act of defiance into a greeting-card sentiment.
detailsBody: In the 1952 translation the surrounding lines read: “It’s really a wonder that I haven’t dropped all my ideals, because they seem so absurd and impossible to carry out. Yet I keep them, because in spite of everything I still believe that people are really good at heart. I simply can’t build up my hopes on a foundation consisting of confusion, misery, and death.”
